title: Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026
official_title: Making continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2026, full-year appropriations for Agriculture, the Legislative Branch, and Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and extensions of agricultural, health, and veterans programs, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Signed into law on November 12, 2025 as Public Law 119-37 — the deal that ended the record-long October–November 2025 government shutdown. The House passed it 217-212 on September 19, but the Senate rejected cloture more than a dozen times before agreeing 60-40 on November 10; the House concurred in the Senate amendment 222-209 on November 12. It funds most agencies at FY2025 rates through January 30, 2026, with full-year budgets for Agriculture/FDA, the Legislative Branch, and Military Construction-VA, plus health, farm, and veterans extensions.

summary: This is the law that ended the October–November 2025 government shutdown. It keeps most agencies running at last year's levels through January 30, 2026, gives full-year budgets to Agriculture and the FDA, Congress, and military construction and veterans programs, and renews a long list of expiring health, farm, and veterans authorities.
brief: A hybrid funding law that ended the 2025 shutdown — a stopgap for most of government plus full-year appropriations for three areas and broad program extensions.

top_lines.headline: Division A — Stopgap & Shutdown Reversal
subs: Funds most agencies at FY2025 rates through January 30, 2026
Reverses October 2025 layoffs and provides federal worker back pay
$199.68M cap and $200M transfer for the E-7 Wedgetail program

top_lines.headline: Division B — Agriculture & FDA
subs: $107.48B for SNAP food assistance; $37.84B for child nutrition
$8.2B for WIC; $6.96B for the Food and Drug Administration
Full-year funding for USDA farm, rural, and research programs

top_lines.headline: Division C — Legislative Branch
subs: $2.08B for the House of Representatives
$852M for Capitol Police salaries and expenses
$811.89M for the Government Accountability Office

top_lines.headline: Division D — Military Construction & VA
subs: $246.63B advance-funded veterans' compensation and pensions
$59.86B medical services and $38.7B community care, advance-funded
$5.73B Navy and $3.93B Air Force military construction; $15.89B in prior-year VA rescissions

top_lines.headline: Division E — Farm Bill Extension
subs: Extends the 2018 Farm Bill through the later of September 30, 2026
Applied as if enacted September 30, 2025 to cover the lapse

top_lines.headline: Division F — Health Extenders
subs: $1.42B for community health centers through January 30, 2026
Extends Medicare telehealth and rural hospital programs
Delays Medicaid safety-net hospital cuts; renews FDA OTC drug fees

top_lines.headline: Division G — VA Extenders
subs: $660M for supportive services for very low-income veteran families
Extends VA health, benefits, and housing authorities to September 30, 2026

top_lines.headline: Division H — Budget Scorekeeping
subs: Exempts the extender divisions from PAYGO scorecards
Zeroes PAYGO balances at the end of the 119th Congress first session

items.main: A stopgap that funds all agencies not covered by Divisions B–D at FY2025 rates through January 30, 2026, and undoes the October 2025 shutdown.
items.detail: Keeps the rest of the federal government running at last year's spending levels through January 30, 2026, after the October 2025 funding lapse. It ends the shutdown, pays workers their missed wages, and reverses layoffs that agencies started during the gap.

sections.label: Division B — Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agency Appropriations Act, 2026

items.main: A full-year appropriation for USDA, the FDA, and domestic nutrition programs, led by $107.48B for food stamps and $37.84B for child nutrition.
items.detail: Funds the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the Food and Drug Administration, and the country's main food-aid programs for 2026. The biggest pieces are food assistance for low-income families, school meals, and aid for mothers and infants.

sections.label: Division C — Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 2026

items.main: A full-year appropriation for the legislative branch, led by $2.08B for the House of Representatives and roughly $852M for the Capitol Police.
items.detail: Funds Congress itself and its support agencies for 2026 — the House, the Senate, the Capitol Police, the Library of Congress, and government watchdogs. The largest share goes to running the House of Representatives.

sections.label: Division D — Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026

items.main: A full-year appropriation for military construction and the VA, anchored by a $246.63B advance appropriation for veterans' compensation and pensions and $59.86B for VA medical services.
items.detail: Pays for building and maintaining military bases and family housing, and funds the Department of Veterans Affairs — veterans' disability checks, pensions, and medical care. Most of the VA money is set a year ahead so veterans' benefits keep flowing without interruption.

sections.label: Division E — Extension of Agricultural Programs

items.main: Extends the 2018 Farm Bill (Agriculture Improvement Act) and its programs through the later of September 30, 2026.
items.detail: Keeps the 2018 Farm Bill alive by extending its programs and authorities, which had lapsed on September 30, 2025. Without this, dozens of farm, conservation, and rural programs would expire.

items.main: Short-term extensions of public health, Medicare, and Medicaid programs through January 30, 2026, plus a renewal of FDA over-the-counter drug user fees.
items.detail: Keeps a long list of health programs from expiring — community health centers, special diabetes programs, and Medicare rules for rural and home care. Most are extended only to January 30, 2026, the same cliff as the stopgap. It also renews the FDA's fee program for over-the-counter drugs and delays scheduled Medicaid cuts to safety-net hospitals.

sections.label: Division G — Department of Veterans Affairs Extenders

items.main: One-year extensions of VA health, benefits, and housing authorities, including $660M for supportive services for very low-income veteran families.
items.detail: Renews a set of expiring VA authorities covering veterans' health care, benefits, and housing for homeless and disabled veterans. Most simply push expiration dates from September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2026.

items.main: Exempts the extension divisions from PAYGO budget scorecards and zeroes out the scorecard balances.
items.detail: A bookkeeping division that controls how this law's costs are counted against federal budget rules. It keeps the extender divisions from triggering automatic spending cuts.

underreported.summary: Voids reduction-in-force layoffs taken October 1, 2025 through enactment and reinstates affected federal workers with back pay.
underreported.why_unreported: The shutdown-ending law also rolls back layoffs already issued, not just funds forward operations.

underreported.summary: Rescinds $15.89B of prior-year VA medical services funds and $610M of medical support funds even as it adds new advance appropriations.
underreported.why_unreported: A multi-billion-dollar VA health clawback is paired with the new funding.

underreported.summary: Keeps the extender divisions off PAYGO scorecards and zeroes accumulated balances, avoiding an automatic sequestration trigger.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision resets PAYGO balances rather than only changing forward accounting.

criticisms.why: They cut SNAP by 20 percent in the big, ugly bill this summer, dismantled and defunded Federal programs, fired Federal workers, and illegally ignored court orders. This bill fails to address the healthcare crisis, and bipartisan outrage has erupted over language in this bill to pay millions of taxpayer dollars to a handful of Senators whose phone records were subpoenaed in relation to the January 6 investigation. It is a bad bill, and I oppose it.

gaps: Sets a January 30, 2026 funding cliff for most of government while only three areas get full-year budgets.
Many health and farm programs are extended only to late January 2026, recreating the same deadline within weeks.
Delays rather than resolves scheduled Medicaid safety-net hospital cuts and prior-year VA rescissions.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bishop
featured_quotes.text: They cut SNAP by 20 percent in the big, ugly bill this summer, dismantled and defunded Federal programs, fired Federal workers, and illegally ignored court orders. This bill fails to address the healthcare crisis, and bipartisan outrage has erupted over language in this bill to pay millions of taxpayer dollars to a handful of Senators whose phone records were subpoenaed in relation to the January 6 investigation. It is a bad bill, and I oppose it.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Carter
featured_quotes.text: I look forward to reopening the government. The shutdown has gone on long enough, and it is time to end it. Yesterday was Veterans Day. It is a timely reminder of the commitment our Armed Forces personnel have made and the responsibility we have to take care of those who serve our Nation. The military construction and veterans affairs component of the legislation meets that goal. The legislation includes $133.3 billion for the Department of Veterans Affairs, including $113.8 billion in discretionary funding for VA medical care.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Harris
featured_quotes.text: Millions of Americans have suffered because Democrats have refused to reopen the government, harming those who depend on SNAP benefits, Federal workers, Border Patrol agents, and our troops, who were uncertain about their next paycheck. This legislation extends government funding to the end of January 2026, thereby blocking attempts to force a budget-busting omnibus at the last minute before Christmas. It also includes the FY 2026 Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Espaillat
featured_quotes.text: Today's backroom deal does nothing to stop 20 million Americans who will see their healthcare premiums double or triple. It does absolutely nothing to stop provisions in the reconciliation package that will strip 15 million people of their Medicaid coverage. These cuts will have a resounding impact on individuals and the healthcare industry and economy as a whole. Safety net hospitals like Montefiore in my district and federally funded clinics like Boriken in East Harlem face having to eliminate services or completely close.

divisions.label: Division A — Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026
divisions.summary: Keeps the rest of the federal government running at last year's spending levels through January 30, 2026, after the October 2025 funding lapse. It ends the shutdown, pays workers their missed wages, and reverses layoffs that agencies started during the gap.
divisions.brief: A stopgap that funds all agencies not covered by Divisions B–D at FY2025 rates through January 30, 2026, and undoes the October 2025 shutdown.

top_lines.headline: Stopgap Funding Window
subs: Funds continuing projects at FY2025 rates through January 30, 2026
Carries forward the Full-Year CR for 2025 (Public Law 119-4) terms
Time covered deemed to begin October 1, 2025 — covering the lapse

top_lines.headline: Shutdown Reversal & Back Pay
subs: Furloughed federal and grantee employees get full back pay
Layoffs (RIFs) started October 1–enactment are void; workers reinstated
Agencies must notify reinstated employees within 5 days

top_lines.headline: Layoff Freeze During the Stopgap
subs: No federal funds may start or carry out a reduction in force
Exceptions: voluntary separations, court orders, orderly shutdown steps

top_lines.headline: Health & Other Provisions

items.main: Continues FY2025 funding rates for projects not otherwise provided for, under Public Law 119-4 terms.
items.detail: Funds remain available until a full-year 2026 appropriation is enacted or until January 30, 2026, whichever comes first. Defense funds may not start new production or raise production rates above FY2025 levels.

sections.label: Sections 111–119 — Mandatory Payments and Shutdown Cleanup

items.main: Continues mandatory payments and food assistance at current-law levels, and ratifies obligations made during the lapse.
items.detail: The period covered is treated as beginning October 1, 2025, so the division reaches back over the funding gap. Personnel pay, allowances, and benefits are made available for back payments.

items.main: Bars using federal funds to start or carry out layoffs during the stopgap and voids layoffs taken October 1–enactment.
items.detail: Affected employees are reinstated to September 30, 2025 status with the pay they would have earned, including back pay. Agencies must send withdrawal notices within 5 days, stating the reinstatement date and back pay amount.

items.main: Sets specific funding rates and add-ons for defense, justice, security, and health accounts that differ from a flat continuation.
items.detail: Examples include $30M for U.S. Marshals protective operations, a $199.68M cap and $200M transfer for the E-7 Wedgetail program, $237.66M for Treasury terrorism and financial intelligence, $28M for Supreme Court Justice protection, and added Indian Health Service operating funds.

underreported.summary: Retroactively nullifies reduction-in-force actions taken between October 1, 2025 and enactment, reinstating affected workers with back pay.
underreported.why_unreported: Reads as a routine stopgap, but it reverses layoffs already issued during the lapse rather than only funding forward operations.

underreported.summary: Appropriates $174,000 each to the survivors of three Representatives who died in office (from Texas, Arizona, and Virginia).
underreported.why_unreported: Customary death-gratuity payments embedded in a funding bill rather than noted as standalone items.

gaps: Sets a January 30, 2026 cliff without resolving full-year funding for the agencies it continues.
Does not specify total spending for continued programs — amounts track FY2025 rates rather than stated figures.
Bars layoffs during the window but does not address staffing actions after January 30, 2026.

added: $437.46M authorization for a European Bank for Reconstruction and Development capital subscription
modified: Office of Personnel Management salaries figure changed to $197.45M from $219.08M
Millennium Challenge Corporation availability extended to December 31, 2026 from December 31, 2024
removed: Voids reduction-in-force actions taken October 1, 2025 through enactment

$1B for section 502 direct rural housing loans

items.main: Funds USDA research, marketing, and regulatory agencies.
items.detail: Includes $1.79B for the Agricultural Research Service and $1.22B for the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service. The Office of the Secretary receives $46.36M.

sections.label: Title II — Farm Production and Conservation Programs

items.main: Funds farm loan programs, the Farm Service Agency, and conservation operations.
items.detail: The Farm Service Agency receives $1.13B for salaries and expenses. Farm loan levels include $3.5B in guaranteed farm ownership loans and $2.58B in direct farm ownership loans.

items.main: Funds rural housing, business, and utilities programs, mostly through loan authority rather than direct spending.
items.detail: Authorizes $25B in section 502 single-family housing loan guarantees and $1B in section 502 direct loans. Rural business and industry guaranteed loans are set at $1.75B.

items.main: Funds the nation's largest food-assistance programs.
items.detail: The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program receives $107.48B, with $6B held in reserve. Child nutrition gets $37.84B and WIC gets $8.2B, of which $150M is reserved for participation surges.

sections.label: Title V — Foreign Assistance and Related Programs

items.main: Funds international food aid and agricultural trade programs.
items.detail: Food for Peace Title II grants receive $1.2B and McGovern-Dole international food-for-education grants receive $240M. A report on transferring Food for Peace from USAID to USDA is required within 60 days.

sections.label: Title VI — Related Agency and Food and Drug Administration

items.main: Funds the FDA and sets the Farm Credit Administration's spending limit.
items.detail: The FDA receives $6.96B total, including $2.5B for drug evaluation and $1.17B for the Human Foods Program. The Farm Credit Administration is capped at $106.5M in administrative expenses from industry assessments.

underreported.summary: Directs a 60-day report on moving the Food for Peace program from USAID to USDA, with $1M set aside for the interagency review.
underreported.why_unreported: A potential restructuring of U.S. international food aid is embedded as a reporting proviso inside a salaries line.

underreported.summary: Places $6B of SNAP funds in two $3B reserves available only as needed for program operations.
underreported.why_unreported: Reserve structure means the headline appropriation overstates what is immediately spendable.

gaps: Rural Development figures are dominated by loan authority levels that do not equal cash outlays.
Does not set the outcome of the Food for Peace transfer it studies — only orders a report.
FDA funding leans heavily on user fees, leaving program levels exposed if collections fall short.

added: $10M for competitive school-equipment grants within child nutrition
Requirement for a 60-day report on transferring Food for Peace to USDA
modified: School Lunch Act authorization years updated to 2010 through 2027 from 2010 through 2025
WIC cash-value voucher maintained at the National Academies' inflation-adjusted level

sections.label: Title I — Legislative Branch Appropriations (Senate, House, Joint Items)

items.main: Funds the day-to-day operations of the House, Senate, and joint congressional accounts.
items.detail: The House of Representatives receives $2.08B, including $850M for Members' representational allowances. Senate officer and employee salaries are funded at $311.54M.

sections.label: Title I — Capitol Police and Architect of the Capitol

items.main: Funds Capitol security and the upkeep of Capitol complex buildings and grounds.
items.detail: Capitol Police receive $653.42M for salaries and $198.93M for general expenses. Architect of the Capitol security operations are funded at $75.07M.

sections.label: Title I — Library of Congress, GPO, and GAO

items.main: Funds congressional support and oversight agencies.
items.detail: The Government Accountability Office receives $811.89M, the Library of Congress $592.41M, and the Copyright Office $102.39M. The Government Publishing Office is funded for congressional printing and its revolving fund.

items.main: Sets government-wide rules and limits on how legislative branch funds may be used.
items.detail: Bars using funds for maintenance of private vehicles except for emergency assistance, and imposes fiscal-year limitations on the appropriations.

underreported.section: Congressional Office for International Leadership Fund
underreported.summary: Funds the program at $6M but bars using money for officials of the central government of Russia, limiting Russian participants to free-market, humanitarian, and civic activities.
underreported.why_unreported: A Russia-specific spending restriction sits inside a small exchange-program line.

gaps: Does not change the structure of Capitol security despite splitting police funding across salary and expense accounts.
Member office allowances are set as a lump sum without per-office detail in the bill text.
Support-agency funding is set for one year without multi-year planning figures.

modified: Capitol Police overtime capped at $80.07M unless the Appropriations Committees approve more

divisions.label: Division D — Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026
divisions.summary: Pays for building and maintaining military bases and family housing, and funds the Department of Veterans Affairs — veterans' disability checks, pensions, and medical care. Most of the VA money is set a year ahead so veterans' benefits keep flowing without interruption.

items.main: Funds construction and family housing for the military services.
items.detail: Navy and Marine Corps construction receives $5.73B, Air Force $3.93B, Defense-Wide $3.78B, and Army $2.38B. Funds also cover the National Guard, reserves, NATO infrastructure, and base closure accounts.

items.main: Funds disability compensation, pensions, and readjustment benefits, mostly a year in advance.
items.detail: Compensation and pensions receive $5.85B for the remainder of 2026 plus $246.63B available October 1, 2026. Readjustment benefits get $4.88B plus a $24.7B advance, and VBA operating expenses are $3.88B.

items.main: Funds VA medical care, mostly through advance appropriations available October 1, 2026.
items.detail: Medical services receive $59.86B, medical community care $38.7B, medical support and compliance $12B, and medical facilities $11.7B. Of FY2025 funds, $15.89B in medical services and $610M in medical support are rescinded.

items.main: Funds cemeteries, monuments, and the Armed Forces Retirement Home.
items.detail: Arlington National Cemetery receives $118.78M, the American Battle Monuments Commission $110M, and the Armed Forces Retirement Home $80M from its trust fund.

underreported.summary: Rescinds $15.89B of FY2025 VA medical services funds and $610M of medical support funds previously provided by Public Law 119-4.
underreported.why_unreported: A multi-billion-dollar clawback of prior-year VA health funds sits among the new advance appropriations.

underreported.summary: Allocates $6.36B for veterans' homelessness programs and $3.46B for rural health care from designated accounts.
underreported.why_unreported: The homelessness and rural-care set-asides are specified through account-transfer provisions rather than separate headings.

gaps: Most VA funding is advance appropriations for FY2027, so the division does little new spending in the current year.
Does not address the staffing levels needed to deliver the medical care it funds.
Rescinds prior-year medical funds without specifying replacement timing for affected programs.

items.main: Continues 2018 Farm Bill programs and their funding levels until the later of September 30, 2026.

divisions.label: Division F — Health Extenders
divisions.summary: Keeps a long list of health programs from expiring — community health centers, special diabetes programs, and Medicare rules for rural and home care. Most are extended only to January 30, 2026, the same cliff as the stopgap. It also renews the FDA's fee program for over-the-counter drugs and delays scheduled Medicaid cuts to safety-net hospitals.
divisions.brief: Short-term extensions of public health, Medicare, and Medicaid programs through January 30, 2026, plus a renewal of FDA over-the-counter drug user fees.

top_lines.headline: Public Health Extensions
subs: $1.42B for community health centers through January 30, 2026
$115.32M for the National Health Service Corps
$58.49M for teaching health centers running residency programs
$53.15M each for type I and Indian special diabetes programs

top_lines.headline: Medicare Extensions
subs: Extends telehealth flexibilities through January 30, 2026
Extends the Medicare-Dependent and low-volume hospital programs
Extends ambulance add-on payments and the work geographic index floor
$2M for Medicare hospice surveys

top_lines.headline: Medicaid & Safety-Net Hospitals
subs: Delays scheduled disproportionate share hospital cuts to January 31, 2026
$17.75M Tennessee DSH allotment for the stopgap period

top_lines.headline: FDA Drug User Fees
subs: Renews the over-the-counter monograph drug user fee program
Dedicates fees to OTC monograph drug review activities

top_lines.headline: Human Services & Surprise Billing
subs: Extends sexual risk avoidance and personal responsibility education
Extends family-to-family health information centers
$14M to continue No Surprises Act implementation funding

items.main: Extends funding for community health centers and related primary-care programs.
items.detail: Provides $1.42B for community health centers, $115.32M for the National Health Service Corps, and $58.49M for teaching health centers, all for October 1, 2025 through January 30, 2026. Special diabetes programs receive $53.15M each.

items.main: Extends expiring Medicare payment rules and adjusts the Medicare Improvement Fund and sequestration.
items.detail: Telehealth flexibilities, the Medicare-Dependent Hospital program, ambulance add-ons, and the work geographic index floor are extended through late January 2026. The Medicare Improvement Fund is set at $1.4B for fiscal year 2027, down from $1.8B.

items.main: Extends abstinence-related education and family health programs.
items.detail: Sexual Risk Avoidance Education, Personal Responsibility Education, and family-to-family health information centers are funded on a pro-rata basis through January 30, 2026.

items.main: Delays scheduled Medicaid disproportionate share hospital cuts and sets Tennessee's allotment.
items.detail: The DSH allotment reductions are pushed to begin January 31, 2026, and Tennessee's allotment is set at $17.75M for the October 1, 2025 to January 30, 2026 period.

sections.label: Title V — Over-the-Counter Monograph Drug User Fee Amendments

items.main: Renews the FDA's authority to collect and use fees for over-the-counter monograph drugs.
items.detail: Re-establishes the user fee program with dedicated fees for OTC monograph drug review, including new sunset and effective dates.

sections.label: Title VI — No Surprises Act Implementation

items.main: Continues funding to implement the surprise medical billing protections.
items.detail: Extends availability of $14M for No Surprises Act implementation activities.

underreported.summary: Reduces the Medicare Improvement Fund to $1.4B and shifts its availability to fiscal year 2027 from 2026.
underreported.why_unreported: The change reduces a Medicare reserve fund by about $400M alongside the routine extensions.

underreported.summary: Delays statutory disproportionate share hospital cuts rather than eliminating them, pushing the reduction window to begin January 31, 2026.
underreported.why_unreported: The cuts are postponed, not canceled, so safety-net hospitals still face them after the stopgap.

gaps: Most health programs are extended only to January 30, 2026, recreating the same cliff weeks later.
Delays but does not resolve the scheduled Medicaid safety-net hospital cuts.
Reduces the Medicare Improvement Fund without specifying offsetting program changes.

added: $14M continued for No Surprises Act implementation
modified: Medicare Improvement Fund set at $1.4B for FY2027, down from $1.8B
Medicaid DSH allotment reductions delayed to begin January 31, 2026
Medicare sequestration spread shifted to 11 months from 10 months

divisions.label: Division G — Department of Veterans Affairs Extenders
divisions.summary: Renews a set of expiring VA authorities covering veterans' health care, benefits, and housing for homeless and disabled veterans. Most simply push expiration dates from September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2026.
divisions.brief: One-year extensions of VA health, benefits, and housing authorities, including $660M for supportive services for very low-income veteran families.

top_lines.headline: Veteran Housing & Homelessness
subs: $660M for supportive services for very low-income veteran families
Extends homeless women veterans and veterans-with-children grants
Extends specially adapted housing authorities to September 30, 2026

top_lines.headline: VA Health Care Authorities
subs: Extends copayment collection and nursing home care to September 30, 2026
Extends the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox suicide prevention grants
Extends rural veterans mental health network funding

top_lines.headline: Benefits & Other Matters
subs: Extends contract physician disability exam authority to six years
Extends VA Inspector General subpoena authority to September 30, 2026
Improves the VA home loan partial claim program

items.main: Extends VA health care authorities set to expire September 30, 2025.
items.detail: Continues copayment collection, nursing home care for service-connected veterans, the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox suicide prevention grant program, and rural mental health network funding through September 30, 2026.

items.main: Extends veterans' benefits authorities and toxic-exposure oversight.
items.detail: Continues quarterly toxic-exposure presumption briefings through December 31, 2026, extends education benefit restoration for closed schools, and lengthens contract physician disability exam authority to six years.

items.main: Extends VA housing and homelessness programs and sets supportive-services funding.
items.detail: Provides $660M for fiscal year 2026 supportive services for very low-income veteran families in permanent housing, and extends specially adapted housing and homeless-veteran treatment authorities.

items.main: Extends VA oversight, transport, and property authorities.
items.detail: Continues the Inspector General's subpoena authority, the vendee loan program, equitable relief reporting, and real property transfer authority through 2026.

underreported.summary: Changes the VA home loan partial claim program's relationship to the Secretary's loan purchase powers, and is the only provision not applied retroactively to September 30, 2025.
underreported.why_unreported: A substantive home-loan default rule sits among otherwise routine date extensions.

gaps: Provides one-year extensions without permanently authorizing the programs.
Sets supportive-services funding for FY2026 only, leaving future years unaddressed.
Does not expand homeless-veteran programs beyond renewing existing authority.

added: $660M authorized for FY2026 supportive services for very low-income veteran families
modified: Contract physician disability exam authority extended to six years from five
VA home loan partial claim program rules clarified (Section 7307)

divisions.label: Division H — Miscellaneous
divisions.summary: A bookkeeping division that controls how this law's costs are counted against federal budget rules. It keeps the extender divisions from triggering automatic spending cuts.
divisions.brief: Exempts the extension divisions from PAYGO budget scorecards and zeroes out the scorecard balances.

top_lines.headline: Budget Scorekeeping
subs: Keeps Divisions E–H off the statutory and Senate PAYGO scorecards
Zeroes PAYGO scorecard balances at the end of the 119th Congress first session
Bars estimating these divisions' effects for sequestration purposes

items.main: Shields the law's extension divisions from automatic budget enforcement.
items.detail: Directs that the budgetary effects of Divisions E through H not be recorded on PAYGO scorecards and sets those scorecard balances to zero, preventing a sequestration trigger.

underreported.summary: Resets PAYGO scorecard balances to zero at the adjournment of the first session of the 119th Congress.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision erases accumulated PAYGO balances beyond a routine effective-date change.

gaps: Removes budget-enforcement accounting without offsetting the underlying costs.
Applies only to the extender divisions, not the appropriations divisions.
Does not disclose the size of the budgetary effects being exempted.

modified: PAYGO scorecard balances set to zero at end of the 119th Congress first session
removed: Exempts Divisions E–H from PAYGO scorecard entries
